questions.q: Which organism is the most common overall cause of bacterial meningitis in adults?
ch: Neisseria meningitidis
Listeria monocytogenes
Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae)
Staphylococci and gram-negative rods
Streptococcus pneumoniae
questions.exp: Streptococcus pneumoniae is listed as the top adult pathogen and the most common overall cause of bacterial meningitis in adults.
why: Neisseria meningitidis is a leading adult pathogen but ranks behind pneumococcus as the most common overall cause.
Listeria monocytogenes is an add-on concern in age over 50, pregnancy, or immunocompromise rather than the usual adult cause.
Group B Streptococcus is a neonatal pathogen alongside E. coli and Listeria.
Staphylococci and gram-negative rods are the post-neurosurgery and shunt-associated organisms.

questions.q: Which set of findings is the classic triad of bacterial meningitis?
ch: Fever, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status
Fever, papilledema, and photophobia
Headache, petechial rash, and bradycardia
Neck stiffness, new seizure, and hypotension
Fever, focal deficit, and sensorineural hearing loss
questions.exp: The classic triad is fever, neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity), and altered mental status, although all three are present in fewer than half of cases.
why: Papilledema is an indication for CT before lumbar puncture, not a component of the classic triad.
A petechial rash points to meningococcemia and bradycardia belongs to the Cushing triad of raised ICP.
A new seizure is a red flag and a CT-before-LP indication rather than part of the presenting triad.
A focal deficit is a red flag and hearing loss is a later complication, not a presenting triad feature.

questions.q: Which CSF profile is characteristic of bacterial meningitis?
ch: Low opening pressure with a normal cell count and low protein
High opening pressure, neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, and high protein
Normal opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and mildly high protein
Lymphocytic pleocytosis with very low glucose and very high protein
Neutrophilic pleocytosis with normal glucose and normal protein
questions.exp: The bacterial pattern on lumbar puncture is a high opening pressure, neutrophilic pleocytosis often over 1000, low glucose with a CSF:serum ratio under 0.4, and high protein.
why: Opening pressure is high in bacterial meningitis, not low, and the cell count is markedly raised.
That is the viral pattern — lymphocytes with a normal glucose.
Lymphocytes with a very low glucose and high protein fit the TB or fungal pattern.
Bacterial meningitis lowers the CSF glucose and raises the protein, so normal values do not fit.

questions.q: A 74-year-old man presents with fever, neck stiffness, and confusion. Which empiric antibiotic regimen is appropriate?
ch: Vancomycin and acyclovir
Ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and rifampin
Ceftriaxone and vancomycin
Ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and ampicillin
Ceftriaxone alone at meningitic dosing
questions.exp: Above age 50 Listeria coverage is required, and cephalosporins do not cover Listeria, so ampicillin is added to the baseline ceftriaxone and vancomycin.
why: This pairing leaves pneumococcal and meningococcal coverage inadequate for empiric therapy.
Rifampin is used for chemoprophylaxis of close contacts, not as part of the empiric regimen.
Ceftriaxone with vancomycin is the baseline regimen but misses Listeria in a host over 50.
Ceftriaxone alone omits coverage for resistant pneumococcus and for Listeria.

questions.q: Which finding is an indication to obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture in suspected bacterial meningitis?
ch: Nuchal rigidity on examination
A petechial rash over the trunk
Papilledema on fundoscopic examination
Fever above 39 degrees Celsius
A positive Kernig sign
questions.exp: CT head before lumbar puncture is obtained for focal deficit, new seizure, papilledema, immunocompromise, or reduced GCS because of herniation risk.
why: Nuchal rigidity is an expected meningismus sign and does not by itself raise herniation concern.
A petechial rash strongly suggests meningococcemia but is not one of the imaging indications.
Fever is part of the classic triad and is not an indication for imaging before the tap.
A positive Kernig sign is a low-sensitivity meningismus sign, not a marker of herniation risk.

questions.q: When should dexamethasone be given in suspected pneumococcal meningitis?
ch: Only once CSF culture confirms pneumococcus
Only if the patient develops hearing loss
Only after the CT head has been completed
Before or with the first antibiotic dose
Twenty-four hours after antibiotics have started
questions.exp: Dexamethasone is given before or with the first antibiotic dose in suspected pneumococcal meningitis to reduce hearing loss and mortality, and is discontinued if pneumococcus is excluded.
why: Waiting for culture confirmation delays it past the window; it is started empirically and stopped if pneumococcus is excluded.
Dexamethasone is given to prevent hearing loss, not as a rescue after hearing loss appears.
Neither antibiotics nor dexamethasone should wait for imaging in a suspected case.
Delaying the steroid until the next day forfeits the benefit, which depends on giving it with the first dose.

questions.q: A patient with suspected Neisseria meningitidis meningitis is admitted. Which infection-control measure is required?
ch: Droplet precautions until at least 24 hours of effective antibiotics
Contact precautions only, until the petechial rash has fully resolved
Standard precautions only, because the organism is not transmissible
Protective isolation to shield the patient from other hospital infections
Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room until cultures are final
questions.exp: Droplet precautions are initiated for suspected Neisseria meningitidis and continued until the patient has had at least 24 hours of effective antibiotics.
why: Contact precautions do not address droplet spread, and the rash is not the criterion for stopping isolation.
Meningococcus is transmissible to close contacts, who also need chemoprophylaxis.
The purpose is to protect staff and other patients from the patient, not the reverse.
Airborne precautions are not what the meningococcal protocol calls for; droplet precautions are the standard.

questions.q: A patient admitted with bacterial meningitis develops rising blood pressure with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular respirations. What does this indicate?
ch: SIADH with dilutional hyponatremia
Impending herniation from raised intracranial pressure
Early septic shock from meningococcemia
A drug reaction to vancomycin
Hypoglycemia caused by dexamethasone
questions.exp: Widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular respirations are the Cushing triad of rising ICP, signalling impending herniation.
why: SIADH is a recognized complication but causes hyponatremia, not the Cushing triad.
Septic shock presents with hypotension and poor perfusion rather than hypertension with bradycardia.
Vancomycin reactions do not produce this specific triad of vital-sign changes.
Steroid effects on glucose run high, and hypoglycemia would not give this vital-sign pattern.

questions.q: A young adult with fever and rapidly spreading petechiae becomes hypotensive with oozing from IV sites. Which complication should be anticipated?
ch: Communicating hydrocephalus from impaired CSF resorption
SIADH producing dilutional hyponatremia during recovery
Fulminant meningococcemia with DIC and Waterhouse-Friderichsen adrenal hemorrhage
Subdural empyema complicating contiguous spread from sinusitis
Delayed sensorineural hearing loss needing a discharge hearing screen
questions.exp: Rapidly spreading petechiae and purpura with hypotension indicate fulminant meningococcemia — think DIC and Waterhouse-Friderichsen adrenal collapse.
why: Hydrocephalus is a later complication and does not cause coagulopathic bleeding.
SIADH is a complication of meningitis but does not produce purpura, bleeding, or hypotension.
Subdural empyema is a recognized complication but does not explain spreading purpura with bleeding and shock.
Hearing loss is a late complication to screen for at discharge, not the acute emergency here.

questions.q: A patient with suspected meningitis has a new focal deficit, so a CT head is needed before the lumbar puncture. What is the correct sequence?
ch: Perform the LP immediately without imaging to avoid delaying treatment
Give antibiotics only after the CSF Gram stain result has returned
Withhold antibiotics until the CT has excluded a mass lesion
Obtain the CT first, then draw blood cultures, then give antibiotics
Draw blood cultures, give antibiotics, then obtain the CT and the LP
questions.exp: Blood cultures then antibiotics come first; when CT is indicated before the LP the antibiotics are still given first, because the LP can wait and treatment cannot.
why: A focal deficit makes an immediate tap unsafe because of herniation risk, so imaging is required first.
Waiting for the Gram stain delays empiric therapy that should already be running.
Antibiotics are never withheld while imaging is pending in a suspected case.
Imaging before antibiotics delays treatment, and door-to-antibiotic time drives mortality.

questions.q: Which statement defines status epilepticus at the operational t1 threshold?
ch: A seizure lasting 30 minutes or longer, regardless of recovery between events
Two or more seizures within a single 24-hour period with full recovery between them
A convulsion followed by more than one hour of post-ictal confusion
A seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, or two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between them
Any seizure occurring in a patient with an established diagnosis of epilepsy
questions.exp: Status epilepticus at t1 is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer, or two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness between them; t2 at 30 minutes is when long-term neuronal injury begins.
why: Thirty minutes is the t2 threshold for neuronal injury, not the operational t1 that triggers treatment.
Recovery of consciousness between events is exactly what excludes status epilepticus.
Prolonged post-ictal confusion is expected after a convulsion and is not the definition.
Epilepsy means recurrent unprovoked seizures; it does not by itself define status epilepticus.

questions.q: Which agent is first-line to abort an actively seizing patient who already has IV access?
ch: IV levetiracetam
IV fosphenytoin
IV valproate
IV propofol infusion
IV lorazepam
questions.exp: IV lorazepam is the first-line benzodiazepine for emergent abortive therapy, enhancing GABA-A chloride conductance to halt the discharge.
why: Levetiracetam is a second-line urgent-control agent given after the benzodiazepine, not the abortive drug.
Fosphenytoin is second-line urgent control and needs cardiac monitoring; it does not replace the benzodiazepine.
Valproate is a second-line option after the benzodiazepine and is avoided in pregnancy.
Propofol is a third-line anesthetic infusion for refractory status requiring intubation and cEEG.

questions.q: What should be checked first in every seizing patient?
ch: Continuous EEG
Fingerstick glucose
Serum prolactin
Head CT
AED drug levels
questions.exp: Check a glucose on every seizing patient before anything else, because hypoglycemia is instantly reversible; the immediate fingerstick glucose precedes electrolytes, toxicology, and imaging.
why: Continuous EEG is for status that does not wake up, not the first bedside action.
Prolactin supports a seizure over a psychogenic event afterwards; it is not the immediate first test.
Imaging follows the immediate bedside glucose and does not come before it.
AED levels matter in a known epileptic but are drawn with the other labs, after the glucose.

questions.q: A patient is convulsing in the field and IV access cannot be obtained. Which rescue therapy is preferred?
ch: Rectal valproate as a loading dose
IM midazolam
IV lorazepam once access is finally achieved
Oral levetiracetam given between convulsions
IV fosphenytoin through an intraosseous line
questions.exp: IM midazolam is first-line when there is no IV access, is rapidly absorbed prehospital, and was supported by the RAMPART trial.
why: Rectal rescue in the community uses diazepam or midazolam, not valproate.
Waiting for IV access delays the benzodiazepine, and delay is what makes status harder to stop.
An actively convulsing patient cannot safely take oral medication.
Fosphenytoin is a second-line agent and does not substitute for the first-line benzodiazepine.

questions.q: After an adequately dosed benzodiazepine, which statement about second-line urgent control is correct?
ch: No second-line agent is needed once the benzodiazepine has worked
Levetiracetam requires cardiac monitoring for bradyarrhythmia risk
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate are roughly equal in efficacy
Fosphenytoin is clearly superior and should always be chosen first
Valproate is the preferred agent in pregnancy because it is well tolerated
questions.exp: ESETT showed levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate are roughly equal in efficacy as second-line agents given after a benzodiazepine to prevent recurrence.
why: A second-line agent is loaded after the benzodiazepine precisely to prevent recurrence.
Cardiac monitoring belongs to fosphenytoin; levetiracetam's cautions are neuropsychiatric and mood effects.
The three second-line agents performed about equally, so no clear superiority justifies always choosing one.
Valproate is specifically avoided in pregnancy and carries hepatotoxicity and hyperammonemia risk.

questions.q: A patient begins a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in bed. Which nursing action is appropriate?
ch: Insert a padded tongue blade to protect the airway and the teeth
Restrain the limbs firmly to prevent injury from the convulsion
Leave the bedside to summon help and return with the crash cart
Sit the patient upright and give oral glucose immediately
Turn the patient to the side, protect the head, and time the seizure
questions.exp: Safety first: protect the head, remove hazards, turn the patient to the side in the recovery position, and time the seizure while preparing suction and oxygen.
why: Nothing is ever inserted in the mouth of a seizing patient.
The limbs are not restrained; restraint causes injury rather than preventing it.
The patient is not left alone during a seizure.
Nothing is given by mouth during a convulsion, and the side-lying recovery position is what protects the airway.

questions.q: After a witnessed convulsion a patient has transient right-arm weakness that resolves over several hours. What is the most likely explanation?
ch: A psychogenic nonepileptic event
Propofol infusion syndrome
Todd's paralysis
An acute ischemic stroke in evolution
Ongoing nonconvulsive status epilepticus
questions.exp: Todd's paralysis is transient focal weakness after a seizure that mimics stroke but resolves within hours.
why: A psychogenic event is suggested by anterior tongue-tip biting and rapid recovery, not post-ictal focal weakness.
Propofol infusion syndrome involves acidosis and rhabdomyolysis with prolonged high-dose infusion.
A stroke deficit would not be expected to resolve completely within hours after a witnessed convulsion.
Nonconvulsive status is suspected when the patient does not wake up, not when a focal weakness clears.

questions.q: Convulsions stopped 40 minutes ago after lorazepam and levetiracetam, but the patient still does not wake up. What is the priority?
ch: Repeat the levetiracetam dose and reassess in another hour
Order a lumbar puncture before any further neurologic monitoring
Start a propofol infusion empirically without any EEG monitoring
Obtain continuous EEG to look for nonconvulsive status epilepticus
Assume a prolonged post-ictal state and simply observe overnight
questions.exp: A patient who does not return to baseline after convulsions stop may be in nonconvulsive status epilepticus, and continuous EEG is required to diagnose it and guide therapy.
why: Repeating a dose without knowing whether seizures continue electrically leaves the diagnosis unmade.
Lumbar puncture is indicated for fever or meningismus; it does not answer whether seizures are ongoing.
Anesthetic infusions require intubation and cEEG-guided titration, not empiric use without monitoring.
Assuming a post-ictal state is the classic way nonconvulsive status is missed.

questions.q: A patient in status epilepticus fails benzodiazepines and a full second-line load. Which reversible cause deserves active consideration?
ch: INH (isoniazid) toxicity, treated with pyridoxine
Chronic migraine with aura
Benign essential tremor
Peripheral neuropathy from B12 deficiency
A simple febrile convulsion of childhood
questions.exp: Refractory status epilepticus unresponsive to standard medications should prompt thought of INH toxicity, treated with pyridoxine, as well as autoimmune anti-NMDA encephalitis or eclampsia treated with magnesium.
why: Migraine is not among the listed triggers of status epilepticus and does not explain refractoriness.
Essential tremor is a movement disorder and has no role in refractory status epilepticus.
Peripheral neuropathy is not a cause of ongoing cortical seizure activity.
A febrile convulsion of childhood does not explain refractory status in this setting.

questions.q: A woman at 32 weeks of pregnancy has a generalized convulsion. What is the immediate treatment priority?
ch: Magnesium sulfate for eclampsia with obstetric emergency management
An IV valproate load as the urgent-control agent
Oral levetiracetam started at a low maintenance dose
Observation alone, since seizures in pregnancy are usually benign
Rectal diazepam only, avoiding all intravenous therapy
questions.exp: A seizure in a pregnant patient beyond 20 weeks is treated as eclampsia with magnesium sulfate and obstetric emergency management.
why: Valproate is specifically avoided in pregnancy because of its teratogenic and hepatic risks.
A low oral maintenance dose does nothing for an acute convulsion in a pregnant patient.
A seizure after 20 weeks is a red flag for eclampsia, never something to observe.
Rectal rescue is a community measure and does not replace magnesium in suspected eclampsia.

questions.q: What is the pathologic hallmark of Parkinson's disease?
ch: Extracellular amyloid plaques with neuritic degeneration
Hyperphosphorylated tau neurofibrillary tangles in the cortex
Inflammatory demyelinating plaques with oligodendrocyte loss
Spongiform vacuolation with prion protein deposition
Intraneuronal Lewy bodies composed of aggregated alpha-synuclein
questions.exp: The pathologic hallmark of Parkinson's disease is the intraneuronal Lewy body, composed of aggregated alpha-synuclein, accompanying loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.
why: Amyloid plaques are a feature of Alzheimer pathology, not the hallmark of Parkinson's disease.
Tau neurofibrillary tangles belong to Alzheimer pathology rather than to nigral degeneration.
Demyelinating plaques describe an inflammatory demyelinating disease, not nigral neuron loss.
Spongiform change with prion deposition describes a rapidly progressive prion disease.

questions.q: The TRAP mnemonic summarizes the cardinal motor features of Parkinson's disease. What does it stand for?
ch: Tremor, reflex loss, athetosis, and ptosis of the eyelids
Resting tremor, rigidity, akinesia/bradykinesia, and postural instability
Intention tremor, rigidity, ataxia, and progressive paralysis
Resting tremor, restlessness, apraxia, and painful paresthesia
Titubation, rigidity, aphasia, and photophobia on exposure
questions.exp: TRAP is resting Tremor, cogwheel Rigidity, Akinesia/bradykinesia, and Postural instability — the classic tetrad of Parkinson's disease.
why: Reflex loss, athetosis, and ptosis do not appear in the cardinal motor tetrad.
The tremor of Parkinson's disease is a resting tremor, and ataxia is not one of the cardinal features.
Restlessness, apraxia, and paresthesia are not part of the described tetrad.
Titubation, aphasia, and photophobia are not cardinal motor features of the disease.

questions.q: Which tremor description fits Parkinson's disease?
ch: A 4-6 Hz pill-rolling resting tremor that improves with movement
A high-frequency intention tremor that worsens as the target is approached
A postural tremor of the hands that improves markedly with alcohol
A head-nodding tremor that is present only during sleep
A symmetric tremor appearing only during sustained physical exertion
questions.exp: Parkinson's disease produces a 4-6 Hz pill-rolling resting tremor that improves with movement, the opposite of an intention or cerebellar tremor.
why: A tremor that worsens on approaching a target is an intention or cerebellar tremor, the opposite pattern.
An alcohol-responsive postural tremor is not the resting tremor described in this module.
The parkinsonian tremor is a resting tremor of the awake limb, not a sleep phenomenon.
Onset is characteristically asymmetric, and the tremor is present at rest rather than only with exertion.

questions.q: Under the MDS diagnostic criteria, what is required to diagnose Parkinson's disease?
ch: Bradykinesia plus resting tremor and/or rigidity
An abnormal DaTscan result in every patient
MRI evidence of substantia nigra atrophy
A positive alpha-synuclein blood test
Postural instability as the earliest feature
questions.exp: Parkinson's disease is a clinical diagnosis: bradykinesia plus resting tremor and/or rigidity per the MDS diagnostic criteria, with a robust sustained levodopa response as a supportive criterion.
why: DaTscan is reserved for confirming a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit when the diagnosis is unclear.
MRI is typically normal and is done to exclude structural and vascular mimics.
There is no such diagnostic blood test in the criteria described here.
Postural instability is part of the tetrad but early falls are actually a red flag for Parkinson-plus.

questions.q: A patient started on pramipexole develops new compulsive gambling. What does this represent?
ch: Levodopa-induced dyskinesia requiring amantadine
Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia from abrupt drug withdrawal
Anticholinergic confusion from trihexyphenidyl
An impulse control disorder from the dopamine agonist
A wearing-off phenomenon between levodopa doses
questions.exp: Dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole carry a risk of impulse control disorders including gambling and hypersexuality, along with sleep attacks and hallucinations.
why: Dyskinesia is involuntary movement from levodopa, not a compulsive behavior.
Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia follows abrupt levodopa withdrawal with fever and rigidity.
Anticholinergics cause confusion and memory loss in the elderly, not compulsive gambling.
Wearing-off is a return of motor symptoms before the next dose, not a behavioral compulsion.

questions.q: Which nursing action best supports a hospitalized patient taking carbidopa-levodopa?
ch: Substitute metoclopramide whenever the patient reports nausea
Stop levodopa for 24 hours before any scheduled procedure
Give levodopa on time, every time, and separate doses from high-protein meals
Hold the morning dose until the patient is fully awake and oriented
Crush and combine all of the daily doses into one morning dose
questions.exp: Levodopa must be given on time, every time, because missed or late doses cause severe off periods, and high-protein meals can reduce its absorption.
why: Metoclopramide is a dopamine blocker that causes drug-induced parkinsonism and should be avoided.
Levodopa is never stopped abruptly because of the risk of a parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia crisis.
Holding a dose creates exactly the off period that on-time dosing is meant to prevent.
Combining doses destroys the dosing schedule that keeps motor symptoms controlled.

questions.q: An older adult taking metoclopramide develops symmetric rigidity and bradykinesia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ch: Progressive supranuclear palsy with early falls
Multiple system atrophy with early autonomic failure
Corticobasal degeneration with limb apraxia
Drug-induced parkinsonism from dopamine blockade
Idiopathic Parkinson's disease with asymmetric onset
questions.exp: Antipsychotics and metoclopramide are dopamine blockers that cause drug-induced parkinsonism, which is characteristically symmetric — always review the medication list.
why: Progressive supranuclear palsy is a Parkinson-plus syndrome, not a medication effect.
Multiple system atrophy is a Parkinson-plus syndrome with early autonomic failure, not drug-induced.
Corticobasal degeneration is another Parkinson-plus syndrome rather than a drug effect.
Idiopathic disease is characteristically asymmetric at onset and is not explained by a dopamine blocker.

questions.q: A hospitalized patient's levodopa is withheld for three days. He becomes febrile and rigid with confusion and unstable vital signs. What has happened?
ch: Orthostatic hypotension causing syncope and falls
Levodopa-induced dyskinesia from over-treatment
Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome from abrupt levodopa withdrawal
Serotonin syndrome from an MAO-B inhibitor interaction
Aspiration pneumonia from progressive dysphagia
questions.exp: Abruptly stopping levodopa risks parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia, a neuroleptic malignant syndrome-like crisis with fever, rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability.
why: Orthostatic hypotension causes falls and syncope, not fever with rigidity.
Dyskinesia is an excess-movement complication of levodopa, not a withdrawal crisis.
Serotonin syndrome relates to MAO-B inhibitors combined with meperidine or SSRIs, not to withholding levodopa.
Aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death in this disease but would not follow from stopping the drug.

questions.q: A patient with Parkinson's disease develops distressing visual hallucinations. Which antipsychotic choice is appropriate?
ch: Chlorpromazine given at bedtime nightly
Quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin
Haloperidol, a high-potency typical agent
Fluphenazine given as a depot injection
Risperidone titrated to a high daily dose
questions.exp: Typical antipsychotics are avoided in Parkinson's disease psychosis; quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin are used because their minimal D2 blockade avoids worsening motor symptoms.
why: Chlorpromazine is a typical antipsychotic and blocks dopamine, so it is avoided here.
Haloperidol is a high-potency dopamine blocker that will worsen the motor symptoms.
Depot fluphenazine is a typical antipsychotic and its long duration makes the motor worsening harder to reverse.
Higher-dose risperidone brings substantial D2 blockade and worsens parkinsonism.

questions.q: Why is the onset of Parkinson's disease symptoms so insidious?
ch: The blood-brain barrier delays the delivery of endogenous dopamine
Lewy bodies only begin to form after the motor symptoms have started
Cortical compensation completely prevents any tremor until very late
Dopamine receptors are progressively upregulated throughout the cortex
Symptoms appear only after roughly 60-80% of nigrostriatal neurons are lost
questions.exp: Symptoms emerge only after roughly 60-80% of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons are lost, which explains the insidious onset and drives interest in neuroprotection.
why: The barrier issue concerns getting levodopa into the brain, not the timing of symptom onset.
Lewy bodies are the pathologic hallmark of the underlying degeneration, not a later consequence.
Tremor is one of the cardinal presenting features rather than something suppressed until late.
Receptor upregulation in the cortex is not the explanation given for the delayed presentation.

questions.q: Which pathologic changes define Alzheimer's disease?
ch: Intraneuronal Lewy bodies composed of aggregated alpha-synuclein
Multiple cortical and subcortical infarcts accumulating in a stepwise way
Focal frontal and temporal lobar atrophy with early personality change
Spongiform change with prion protein deposition and prominent myoclonus
Extracellular amyloid plaques and intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau tangles
questions.exp: Alzheimer's disease is defined by extracellular amyloid plaques plus intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau tangles, with cholinergic neuron loss and hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy.
why: Lewy bodies of alpha-synuclein characterize Lewy body dementia with its fluctuating cognition and hallucinations.
Accumulating infarcts with stepwise decline describe vascular dementia rather than Alzheimer pathology.
Early personality and language change with lobar atrophy describes frontotemporal dementia.
Prion pathology with myoclonus suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a rapidly progressive dementia.

questions.q: Which feature best distinguishes delirium from dementia?
ch: Prominent early personality and language change
Acute onset with a fluctuating course and inattention
Gradual decline over years with attention preserved
Loss of smell with REM sleep behavior disorder
Stepwise decline with focal neurologic deficits
questions.exp: Delirium is acute and fluctuating with inattention and is potentially reversible, whereas dementia is a chronic acquired loss of cognition that impairs independence.
why: Early personality and language change points to frontotemporal dementia.
A gradual decline over years describes dementia itself, not delirium.
Hyposmia with REM sleep behavior disorder points toward Lewy body pathology rather than delirium.
Stepwise decline with focal deficits suggests vascular dementia, not an acute confusional state.

questions.q: What is the hallmark early clinical feature of Alzheimer's disease?
ch: Prominent visual hallucinations
Magnetic gait with incontinence
Disinhibited social behavior
Stepwise motor deficits
Short-term (episodic) memory loss
questions.exp: The hallmark early feature of Alzheimer's disease is short-term or episodic memory loss, localizing to the hippocampus and temporal lobe.
why: Visual hallucinations with fluctuating cognition point to Lewy body dementia.
A magnetic gait with incontinence belongs to the normal pressure hydrocephalus triad.
Disinhibited behavior and early personality change point to frontotemporal dementia.
Stepwise decline with focal deficits suggests a vascular cause.

questions.q: Which laboratory tests are obtained mainly to catch reversible causes of cognitive decline?
ch: Amyloid PET imaging
Plasma p-tau217
APOE genotyping
TSH and vitamin B12
CSF amyloid and tau
questions.exp: TSH and vitamin B12 are drawn to exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline, along with CBC, CMP, and RPR or HIV testing when indicated.
why: Amyloid PET is a specialty biomarker rather than a test for reversible mimics.
Plasma p-tau217 is an emerging Alzheimer biomarker, not a reversible-cause screen.
APOE genotyping reflects risk and ARIA susceptibility rather than a treatable cause.
CSF amyloid and tau are biomarkers supporting an Alzheimer diagnosis, not a screen for reversible causes.

questions.q: A patient with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism becomes agitated overnight. Which order should be challenged?
ch: A review of the medication list
Haloperidol for agitation
A structured routine with reorientation cues
Evaluation for pain, infection, or constipation
A low-dose cholinesterase inhibitor
questions.exp: These features describe Lewy body dementia, in which severe neuroleptic sensitivity makes a high-potency antipsychotic such as haloperidol potentially fatal.
why: Reviewing the medication list is a sound step in evaluating new agitation.
A structured routine with reorientation is appropriate first-line non-pharmacologic care.
Identifying triggers such as pain, infection, or constipation is exactly what should be done first.
Cholinesterase inhibitors are used in Lewy body dementia and are a reasonable order.

questions.q: What is first-line management of behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia?
ch: A scheduled benzodiazepine given at bedtime nightly
An anticholinergic agent for restlessness and pacing
Physical restraints applied during agitated episodes
Non-pharmacologic care with a structured routine and environmental modification
An atypical antipsychotic started at the lowest dose
questions.exp: Non-pharmacologic care — structured routine, reorientation, and environmental modification — is first-line for behavioral and psychological symptoms, and triggers such as pain, infection, constipation, and sensory deficits are identified before any medication is added.
why: A nightly benzodiazepine adds sedation and fall risk without addressing the trigger.
Anticholinergic burden worsens confusion in this population.
Restraints do not address the underlying trigger and add injury risk.
Antipsychotics are reserved for severe agitation or psychosis after non-drug measures fail, and carry a black box warning of increased mortality.

questions.q: A patient started on donepezil should be monitored for which adverse effect?
ch: Extrapyramidal rigidity and tremor
Photosensitivity rash on the face
Bradycardia with syncope and GI upset
Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities
Hyponatremia from renal salt wasting
questions.exp: Cholinesterase inhibitors produce cholinergic effects including bradycardia, syncope, GI upset, and weight loss, so monitor heart rate, GI tolerance, and weight.
why: Extrapyramidal effects are an antipsychotic concern, especially in Lewy body dementia.
Photosensitivity is not among the described adverse effects of this drug class.
ARIA is monitored with serial MRI for anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies, not for donepezil.
Hyponatremia is a monitoring point for SSRIs in this population rather than for cholinesterase inhibitors.

questions.q: An older adult has urinary incontinence, cognitive decline, and a magnetic gait. Which diagnosis is potentially reversible?
ch: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
Alzheimer's disease
Frontotemporal dementia
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
Lewy body dementia
questions.exp: The wet, wacky, wobbly triad of urinary incontinence, cognitive decline, and magnetic gait is normal pressure hydrocephalus, which is potentially reversible with shunting.
why: Alzheimer's disease presents with episodic memory loss and is not reversible with a procedure.
Frontotemporal dementia presents with early personality and language change at a younger age.
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, not a reversible cause.
Lewy body dementia features fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism.

questions.q: A patient with early Alzheimer's disease and confirmed amyloid begins lecanemab. What monitoring is required?
ch: Serial MRI for ARIA
Serial ECGs for QT prolongation
Monthly TSH measurement
Weekly liver function tests
Annual DaTscan imaging
questions.exp: Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies require surveillance MRI for ARIA — amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or hemorrhage — and the risk is higher in APOE carriers.
why: QT monitoring relates to citalopram dosing in the elderly, not to anti-amyloid antibodies.
TSH is a one-time screen for a reversible cause rather than ongoing therapy monitoring.
Liver testing is not the monitoring requirement described for this drug class.
DaTscan is a movement-disorder study and has no role in monitoring this therapy.

questions.q: How is Lewy body dementia distinguished from Parkinson disease dementia?
ch: The complete absence of any visual hallucinations
A stepwise decline accompanied by focal deficits
Cognitive decline before or within about a year of parkinsonism
Cognitive decline appearing many years after the motor symptoms
The presence of a resting tremor at the time of onset
questions.exp: Cognitive decline before or within about one year of parkinsonism indicates Lewy body dementia, whereas motor symptoms preceding cognition by years indicates Parkinson disease dementia.
why: Visual hallucinations are a core feature of Lewy body dementia rather than being absent.
Stepwise decline with focal deficits points to vascular dementia.
Motor symptoms first by years is the pattern that defines Parkinson disease dementia instead.
A resting tremor occurs in both and does not separate the two diagnoses.

questions.q: What is the hallmark of multiple sclerosis pathology?
ch: Degeneration of the anterior horn cells
Amyloid deposition in cortical vessels
Lesions disseminated in space and in time
A single monophasic demyelinating event
Demyelination confined to peripheral nerves
questions.exp: The hallmark of multiple sclerosis is separation of lesions in space, meaning multiple CNS sites, and in time, meaning episodes over time.
why: Anterior horn cell degeneration is a motor neuron process, not an inflammatory demyelinating one.
Amyloid in cortical vessels is unrelated to immune-mediated CNS demyelination.
A single monophasic event is a clinically isolated syndrome, which by itself lacks dissemination in time.
Multiple sclerosis attacks CNS myelin and oligodendrocytes, not peripheral nerves.

questions.q: Which risk-factor profile is most typical of multiple sclerosis?
ch: Female, age 20-40, higher latitude, low vitamin D, and prior EBV infection
Male, age over 65, low latitude, and high vitamin D levels
Female, age over 70, with hypertension and long-standing diabetes
Male, childhood onset, with a documented measles infection
Either sex, age 40-60, with heavy alcohol use and smoking
questions.exp: Risk factors include female sex at roughly 3:1, age 20-40, higher latitude with low vitamin D, EBV infection, smoking, and the HLA-DRB1 genetic association.
why: Male sex, older age, and high vitamin D run opposite to the described risk profile.
Onset after 70 with vascular comorbidity does not match the 20-40 age window.
Childhood male onset after measles is not the described epidemiologic pattern; EBV is the implicated virus.
The peak age is 20-40 with a female predominance rather than an even distribution at 40-60.

questions.q: Which disease course accounts for about 85% of multiple sclerosis?
ch: Primary progressive MS
Secondary progressive MS
Radiologically isolated syndrome
Clinically isolated syndrome
Relapsing-remitting MS
questions.exp: Relapsing-remitting MS is the most common disease course in multiple sclerosis, making up about 85%.
why: Primary progressive disease is a separate, less common course, and ocrelizumab is its only approved therapy.
Secondary progressive disease follows an initial relapsing-remitting course rather than accounting for most cases.
A radiologically isolated syndrome is an incidental imaging category, not the dominant course.
A clinically isolated syndrome is a first attack, not an established disease course.

questions.q: Which investigation is the key test for diagnosing multiple sclerosis?
ch: Serum creatine kinase and aldolase levels
Muscle biopsy taken from the quadriceps
MRI brain and spinal cord with gadolinium
CT head without contrast to exclude a mass
Nerve conduction studies of all four limbs
questions.exp: MRI of the brain and spinal cord with gadolinium is the key test, showing periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, and cord lesions with Dawson fingers, while enhancing lesions imply active disease.
why: Muscle enzymes assess myopathy and have no role in establishing this diagnosis.
Muscle biopsy investigates primary muscle disease, not CNS demyelination.
CT lacks the sensitivity to show demyelinating plaques and is not the diagnostic study.
Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerve, whereas this disease is a CNS process.

questions.q: Under the 2017 McDonald criteria, what can CSF oligoclonal bands substitute for?
ch: Dissemination in time
Dissemination in space
A positive AQP4 antibody
An abnormal EDSS score
A gadolinium-enhancing lesion
questions.exp: Under the 2017 McDonald criteria, CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time in a clinically isolated syndrome.
why: Dissemination in space is shown by lesions at multiple CNS sites on MRI, not by oligoclonal bands.
AQP4 antibody testing is used to exclude NMOSD, a mimic, not to satisfy the criteria.
The EDSS tracks disability over time and plays no part in making the diagnosis.
Enhancing lesions indicate activity but are not what the bands replace in the criteria.

questions.q: Which teaching point addresses the Uhthoff phenomenon?
ch: Restrict fluid intake to reduce neurogenic bladder urgency
Avoid hot baths, saunas, and overheating, and use cooling strategies
Avoid all physical exercise permanently to prevent relapse
Sleep in a warm room in order to reduce night-time spasticity
Take hot showers to relieve neuropathic pain in the limbs
questions.exp: The Uhthoff phenomenon is transient worsening with heat, so teach heat avoidance — hot baths, saunas, fever, and overheating — along with cooling strategies.
why: Fluid restriction is not the recommended bladder strategy and does not concern heat sensitivity.
Exercise is encouraged rather than avoided; the specific issue is overheating.
Deliberately warming the sleeping environment worsens symptoms in a heat-sensitive patient.
Hot showers are precisely what triggers the transient worsening being taught about.

questions.q: A patient with known MS presents with a new episode of painful monocular vision loss. What is first-line treatment for the relapse?
ch: Start ocrelizumab that same day
Begin dalfampridine for walking
Give baclofen for spasticity
Start teriflunomide immediately
High-dose IV methylprednisolone
questions.exp: High-dose IV methylprednisolone is first-line for an acute relapse to speed recovery, although it does not change long-term disability; plasma exchange is used for steroid-refractory severe relapses.
why: Ocrelizumab is a disease-modifying therapy to prevent future relapses, not the acute relapse treatment.
Dalfampridine is symptomatic therapy for walking speed and does nothing for an acute attack.
Baclofen treats spasticity and has no role in aborting a relapse.
Teriflunomide is an oral disease-modifying therapy, not an acute relapse treatment.

questions.q: A patient on natalizumab develops new progressive deficits and cognitive decline. What should be suspected and done?
ch: Treat it as an ordinary relapse with oral baclofen
Reassure the patient and repeat the EDSS in six months
Switch immediately to teriflunomide without any imaging
Suspect PML, stop the drug, and obtain MRI and JCV testing
Increase the natalizumab dose and continue treatment
questions.exp: New progressive deficits, cognitive decline, or focal signs on natalizumab suggest PML from JC virus — stop the drug and obtain MRI and JCV testing.
why: Baclofen treats spasticity and would not address a suspected opportunistic brain infection.
Waiting six months allows a potentially devastating infection to progress unchecked.
Switching therapy without imaging leaves the suspected diagnosis unconfirmed and untreated.
Escalating the drug that carries the PML risk is exactly the wrong move.

questions.q: A patient has bilateral optic neuritis and a longitudinally extensive cord lesion. What must be excluded before choosing a therapy?
ch: Benign fasciculation syndrome, by needle EMG
NMOSD, by testing aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies
Vitamin D deficiency, by a 25-hydroxy level
Migraine with aura, by keeping a headache diary
Carpal tunnel syndrome, by nerve conduction
questions.exp: Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis or bilateral optic neuritis points to NMOSD rather than MS, so check aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies, because the wrong disease-modifying therapy can worsen NMOSD.
why: Fasciculations are a peripheral phenomenon and do not account for optic neuritis.
Low vitamin D is a risk factor but does not explain this lesion pattern or change the immediate therapy decision.
Migraine does not produce a longitudinally extensive cord lesion.
Carpal tunnel syndrome is a peripheral entrapment and is unrelated to CNS demyelination.

questions.q: Which screening is required before starting an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody such as ocrelizumab?
ch: Baseline ECG for bradycardia
Macular OCT for edema
Teriflunomide washout period
Hepatitis B screening
Anti-JCV antibody index
questions.exp: Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies require hepatitis B screening first because of the risk of hepatitis B reactivation, alongside attention to infusion reactions and infection risk, and live vaccines are held.
why: A baseline ECG is required for S1P modulators because of first-dose bradycardia and AV block.
Macular edema surveillance belongs to the S1P modulators rather than to anti-CD20 agents.
A washout for teratogenicity applies to teriflunomide in pregnancy planning.
The anti-JCV antibody index stratifies PML risk for natalizumab, not for anti-CD20 therapy.
